o:
Instability of index i is prefixMax(0..i) − suffixMin(i..n-1); we want the smallest i with instability ≤ k. Precompute suffix minima in one backward pass and a running prefix max in a forward scan, testing each index in O(1). With n ≤ 100 even brute force works, but the prefix/suffix method is the intended pattern.

Example 1: suffix mins are [0,0,1,4]; prefix maxes [5,5,5,5]; scores [5,5,4,1] → first ≤ 3 is index 3. Example 2: all scores are 2 > 1 → -1. Example 3: single element scores 0 ≤ 0 → 0.
k: Suffix minima plus a running prefix max turn each query into O(1).

a.n: Approach 1: Suffix minima + running prefix max
a.i: Build sufMin[i] = min(nums[i..n-1]) backwards; then scan forward maintaining prefMax and return the first i with prefMax − sufMin[i] ≤ k.
s: Forward pass with running prefMax; check the condition per index.
Return the first satisfying index or -1.

a.i: For each index, recompute the prefix max and suffix min with inner loops. Quadratic but trivially correct and fine for n ≤ 100; useful as a reference implementation when testing the linear version.
s: For each i, scan 0..i for the max and i..n-1 for the min.
If max − min ≤ k, return i.
a.t: O(n^2) — each index rescans both sides
a.sp: O(1) extra (O(n) transient slices in the JS/Python one-liners)

w: Use the prefix/suffix method — it is the template for many 'split-point' problems. Pitfalls: mixing up which side takes the max versus the min, and 32-bit overflow when values approach 1e9 (use 64-bit differences in Java/C++). Follow-up: count stable indices, or find the smallest index for every k in a batch of queries (sort queries and sweep).
